newsitem.title: USA: Clinton budget seen holding Medicare premium steady.
newsitem.headline: Clinton budget seen holding Medicare premium steady.

text.p: President Bill Clinton has told aides to draft his new budget without raising Medicare premiums, preferring to hold back such a conciliatory gesture toward the Republicans for now, officials said on Tuesday.

The decision reflects a political calculation that it is better to wait before making any concessions to the Republicans on the divisive question of how to rein in the costly health care programme for the elderly.

The officials, who asked not to be identified, said there had been a debate within the administration between those who wanted to save a conciliatory gesture toward the Republicans until later, and those who preferred to see one made in the president's fiscal 1998 budget proposal, due early next month.

"Part of the issue is at what point do we enter into the picture with some new proposals, concessions," one official said. "Do we move toward the Republicans in the front end, rather than later in the negotiations?"

Medicare, which funds health care for 37 million people, is a politically charged subject because of Clinton's success during the 1996 election campaign in tarring the Republicans for their proposals to reduce the program's costs.

Clinton's use of Medicare in the campaign has generated much bitterness among the Republicans, who have repeatedly said since the election they want a gesture from the White House acknowledging that the programme must be restrained.

Republicans feel Clinton unfairly portrayed their proposal to reduce the growth of Medicare, one of the fastest growing federal programmes, as one that would lead to massive cuts in the highly popular programme.
Administration officials acknowledge that at some point they may need to reach out toward the Republicans on the matter, but are divided on when to do so.
They said the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) had been instructed to draft the fiscal 1998 budget without proposing any increase in Medicare premiums.

Although this decision could theoretically be reversed, there is little time to do so because by law the budget must be released on Feb. 3. The White House has said it would prefer to delay releasing the budget, possibly to Feb. 10, after Clinton's State of the Union address.
Those writing the budget are working under the assumption that "most of the Medicare savings (are) coming out of the provider side, not out of the user side," one official said.
Republicans have argued that one way to hold down the program's cost would be to make Medicare recipients with higher incomes bear more of the costs themselves.

Officials said Clinton's fiscal 1998 budget was expected to propose about $100 billion in Medicare savings over five years, mostly achieved by holding down payments to doctors, hospitals and other health care providers, rather than by raising user payments.

One official said the OMB was also operating under the assumption that Medicare's burgeoning home health care costs will be shifted from the Hospital Insurance trust fund to a separate account with access to general tax revenues.

Republicans, as well as some independent analysts, have criticised this as a gimmick, arguing that while it would help maintain the solvency of the Medicare trust fund, it would not address the underlying issue of curbing the program's growth.

Republican Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, who will be one of Clinton's key interlocutors on the budget, Tuesday strongly warned him against juggling the accounts to find savings, telling reporters: "That would be a total cop-out."
